Y9_W01.big_idea: Before we believe a claim, we ask what kind of claim it is and whether evidence could ever check it.
goals: I can sort claims into fact, opinion, testable and not testable, and explain my choice.
I can use Claim, Evidence, Reasoning and the three-point verdict scale to judge a claim.

flow.what: Groups of 4 at fixed tables; role cards; 'no exams, lots of thinking'
Baseline paper, alone and in silence; read instructions aloud; keep time
Read each statement aloud; students mark one face per statement
Great Wall from the Moon? Vote Yes, No or Not sure; do not reveal
Four kinds of claim, flowchart, CER and the three-point verdict scale
Claim sort: 16 cards on the A3 mat; record on the worksheet
Great Wall evidence, model CER, verdict with a frame; exit ticket

Y9_W01.practical: Groups sort 16 claim cards on an A3 mat into Opinion, Fact, Testable or Not testable and record the sort.
Y9_W01.assessment: Baseline skills check (out of 20, tracker); interest survey (tracker); exit ticket: testable or not testable. No logbook this week

Mark skills checks (out of 20); enter scores and surveys in tracker
File skills checks in class assessment folder; never return before Week 10
Read exit tickets for Week 2 grouping

hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules
watch_out: Skills check and survey are fixed. Short of time: cut Challenge; sort only cards A to L.
'Not testable' is not 'false'. Card J (survey) is testable; card L is not a fact.
Never go through or return the skills check: same paper in Week 10.
Y9_W01.language_note: Frame: 'Our verdict is ___ because ___.' Chinese welcome in the sort and pair talk. Do not explain science words in the skills check.
Y9_W01.next_week: Week 2: how our brains fool us; logbook starts. Print anchoring slips, illusion sheets at 100%, tally sheet

Y9_W02.big_idea: Our brains take shortcuts that can fool us, so scientists measure, compare groups and try to prove their own ideas wrong.
goals: I can show with measurements that my perception can be wrong, and say why scientists measure.
I can explain anchoring and confirmation bias using evidence from today's class tests.

flow.what: Anchoring slips, alone and silent, into group envelopes; retrieval: claim type and three verdicts
Muller-Lyer lines: vote A, B or same; no reveal; teacher quietly sorts slips
Perception versus measurement; what bias means; measure to the nearest mm; no anchoring yet
Pairs predict, then measure the illusions; Core; two Recorders calculate the class means
2-4-6 game: groups test numbers, YES and NO columns; reveal rule, name confirmation bias
Reveal anchoring and class means (true about 6,300 km); pair talk; exit ticket; logbook line

Y9_W02.practical: Pairs predict, then measure three illusions with a ruler (mm); groups play the 2-4-6 rule game.
Y9_W02.assessment: Exit ticket: name a bias and a protection; logbook line; My thinking box (bias reflection, series output)

Collect 24 rulers, calculator, board pen, 6 envelopes, 6 trays
Check 24 logbooks are printed and in the class box (first use)
Read the 2-4-6 script; have the answer key sample data ready
Print slips, cut into 24, stack alternating 1, 2; label 6 envelopes

prep_lines.when: On the day, before the lesson
prep_lines.text: Draw YES and NO columns on the board for the 2-4-6 game

prep_lines.when: On the day, before the lesson
prep_lines.text: Set out rulers, envelopes, group cards; slip pile by door; illusion sheets at front
Clean-up: count 24 rulers back; logbooks into the class box
Read exit tickets and My thinking; keep slips and tally until end of Week 3

If the two means are close (many know 6,300 km), treat it as a result; sample data is in the answer key.
2-4-6: answer only 'Yes' or 'No'; do not reveal the rule or comment on the NO column early.
Y9_W02.language_note: Frame: 'My eyes said ___, but the ruler showed ___.' 'Bias' is any pull in one direction, not an unfair person. Chinese welcome in pair talk.
Y9_W02.next_week: Week 3: ruler-drop fair test with repeats, mean, range; print and laminate method cards, check rulers' 0 cm mark

Y9_W03.big_idea: One result can fool us: repeat, calculate mean and range, and ask if a difference is bigger than normal variation.
goals: I can run a fair ruler-drop test with five repeats per hand and calculate mean and range.
I can conclude whether a difference is big enough to matter, mentioning uncertainty.

flow.what: Two retrieval questions on the back of the worksheet: a bias, a mean
Drop the PRIZE strip for 2 or 3 volunteers; vote: is your dominant hand faster?
Name the variables; demo the ruler drop; conversion table; calculate mean and range
Safety slide; pairs do 5 drops per hand, alternating; convert to seconds; mean and range
Overlap diagram: is the difference bigger than the range? Class count; exit ticket; logbook line

Y9_W03.practical: Pairs drop and catch a 30 cm ruler, 5 tries per hand, alternating; convert cm to seconds; find mean and range.
Y9_W03.assessment: Results table with mean and range; conclusion with uncertainty; spot-check 6 worksheets for range; exit ticket; logbook line

Cut the PRIZE strip and a spare from card; write the prize on it
Check the vocabulary traps: range, mean, reaction not reflex

hazards: Rulers can hit faces or fingers: hold upright and still; never flick, swing or throw
Keep your face away from the ruler when it drops
Sit down for every test
watch_out: Range is one number: students write '0.15 to 0.17' instead of subtracting.
Rhythm drops give impossible catches (under 5 cm): repeat those tries; wait a random 1 to 5 seconds.
Bigger distance means slower, not faster; small differences can be normal variation.
Y9_W03.language_note: Frame: 'The data suggests ___; however, ___.' 'Range' is one number (极差, not 范围). Say numbers in English.
Y9_W03.next_week: Week 4: patterns between two variables. Keep method cards and tables for claim 12 (Week 7); PRIZE winner chooses role first

Y9_W04.big_idea: Two things changing together (correlation) does not prove cause: a hidden third factor or chance may explain it, and graphs can mislead.
goals: I can plot a scatter graph and describe the correlation it shows.
I can explain why correlation does not prove causation, name a confounding variable and fix a misleading graph.

flow.what: Retrieval on the back of the worksheet: mean, range, the three verdicts
Winter graph: do hot drinks cause colds? Vote Yes, No or Not sure
Positive, negative, no correlation; correlation is not causation; confounding variable; three explanations
Matching cards; measure arm span and height by code; class table; plot the scatter graph
Fix the graph in pairs: battery advert, redraw from zero, verdict; exit ticket; logbook

Y9_W04.practical: Groups match pattern cards to hidden factors, measure height and arm span (nearest cm, codes not names) and plot a class scatter graph.
Y9_W04.assessment: Scatter graph (Core); Fix the graph sheets collected; exit ticket (links to skills check question 10); logbook line

Read the answer key and Slide 8 method; decide how codes are given
Choose a clear wall stretch per group, away from windows and radiators

Check Fix the graph sheets; read exit tickets before Week 5

Y9_W04.language_note: Frame: 'This could also be explained by ___.' 'Correlation' and 'cause' are different; plural of 'axis' is 'axes'.
Y9_W04.next_week: Fair trials: control group, blinding, placebo; keep the class data photo for Week 7; prepare Week 5 pens and cards

Y9_W05.big_idea: Fair trials need a control group, a placebo and blinding, and they treat the people who take part honestly and with respect.
goals: I can explain why a fair trial needs a control group, a placebo, blinding and a big sample.
I can compare two groups using means and ranges, give an honest verdict and discuss ethics.

flow.what: Checkpoint in place of the Do Now: alone, in silence, own pens; collect at 10 minutes
Tu Youyou story: should we believe an idea because it is old?
Lucky pen trial by the script: card, study 60 s, count, recall 2 min, mark
Reveal the secret at once; control group, placebo, blind, double-blind, random, sample size
Scores by code on the board; class means and ranges; worksheet Core and Stretch
Ethics debrief, chance to withdraw scores; exit ticket; logbook line; introduce incoming teacher

Y9_W05.practical: Memory trial with identical pens: Code 41 cards say 'Focus Pen', Code 52 is the control; compare means and ranges.
Y9_W05.assessment: Checkpoint out of 12 (tracker, 'W5 checkpoint'); trial results table and worksheet Stretch; exit ticket; logbook line

Y9_W06.big_idea: A simple claim can be hard to test: agree exactly what to measure (an operational definition); different definitions can give different answers.
goals: I can fair test 'hot water freezes faster' (A) or compare cooling (B) and record results.
I can explain an operational definition, how it changes a verdict, and my evidence's limits.

flow.what: Three retrieval questions; keep the 'What does frozen mean?' answers on the board
Mpemba story, 1963, still contested; vote: can hot water freeze faster?
Set-up and safety; teacher pours warm water, groups start timing; operational definitions
A: read tubes, check crystals and solid. B: read cups, plot curves. Results to board
Definition debate; two verdicts (our test, claim in general); exit ticket; logbook line

Y9_W06.assessment: Class results and debate; exit ticket (definition, two meanings of 'frozen', verdict); logbook line; tracker column F

Y9_W07.big_idea: Plan before touching the kit: a testable question, a fair comparison, a justified sample size, and care for safety and participants.
goals: I can turn a claim into a testable question and plan a fair test with a justified sample size.
I can plan ethically for human participants and write a specific risk assessment.

Rulers, 30 cm x12 (2 per group)
Staplers or paper clips x6 (1 per group)
Laminating pouches, A5 x6 (optional)
reuse_items: Week 8 run sheet with teacher notes
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules
Feedback can feel personal: comment on the science, never people or their English
watch_out: Tight lesson: keep to the slide clock; unfinished groups still swap at minute 21.
'A good review only says nice things': it is kind and honest, finds real problems, suggests fixes.
Short of time: minimum 2 comment slips, fix major issues only; draft and review are fixed.
Y9_W09.language_note: Reviewer frame: 'In section ___, ___. This matters because ___. We suggest ___.' 'Review' and 'revise' are not test revision. Chinese talk welcome.
Y9_W09.next_week: Collect every report: judge strands 1 to 5 and prepare certificates; check Week 1 skills check papers and fresh copies

Y9_W10.big_idea: Scientists share verdicts in public, say honestly how sure they are and answer with evidence; ten weeks show how our thinking has grown.
goals: I can present our claim, test, data and verdict in a 2-minute talk, with a confidence level and its reason.
I can answer or ask a question from the floor using evidence, not opinion.

flow.what: Skills check papers face down on desks; name, class, date, tick 'Week 10'
Same paper as Week 1: alone, silent; 5-minute warning; collect at once into envelope
Chair welcomes delegates; return reports; give out question cards, slips, listener sheets; running order
Six talks: 2 minutes each, bell at 1:45, one question from the floor; mark strand 6
Finish two stars and a wish slip; teacher fills in the verdict wall
Interest survey read aloud (3 min); certificates and close of the series (2 min)

Y9_W10.practical: No practical: each group gives a 2-minute talk with its report graph, then answers one question from the floor.
Y9_W10.assessment: Final skills check (/20, tracker S); survey (U to Z); strand 6 from marking grid, strands 1 to 5 from reports (AC to AH)

prep_lines.text: Print 6 talk frame cards (A5) plus spares, ready for the end of Week 9
Send print job: skills checks, surveys, slips, listener sheets, question cards, teacher sheets
Judge strands 1 to 5 from Week 9 reports; work out provisional awards
Check Week 1 papers are filed; plan the room layout for the Conference
Print certificates on card (both for boundary students); sort by group
Cut question cards, feedback slips and surveys; fill in the running order

prep_lines.when: On the day, before the lesson
prep_lines.text: Skills check paper face down on every desk; poster up; timer, bell, envelopes
Mark skills checks; enter tracker S, U to Z, AC to AH; check awards
Write 24 one-page skills reports; decide Most Improved; remaining certificates
Gallery walk of reports; file papers; return logbooks; kit back to prep room

print_items: Skills check paper x24 (2 sheets each, double-sided; same paper as Week 1)
Interest survey x24 (2 per A4 sheet, cut: 12 sheets)
Listener sheet (worksheet) x24 (1 sheet, double-sided)
Two stars and a wish slips x6 A4 sheets (4 per sheet, cut), plus spares
Audience question cards x2 sheets, A4 card (12 per sheet, cut)
Talk frame card x6, A5, laminated if possible (1 per group), plus spares
Verdict wall poster x1, A3; marking grid x1, A4; close-out checklist x1, A4
Certificates x25, A4 card (1 per student, 1 Most Improved), plus boundary duplicates
Teacher copies: chair's script card (A5), kit card (A5, double-sided)
get_items: Timer and bell (or a phone alarm)
Labelled envelopes for skills checks and surveys (at least 2)
Sticky tape (verdict wall poster)
Clipboard x1 (marking grid)
Laminating pouches, A5 x6 (optional)
Visualiser, if there is one (optional)
Make: running order (poster or slide 4) with each group's claim
reuse_items: Week 1 skills check papers x24 (filed, not returned)
Rubric and skills check mark scheme (teacher copies)
hazards: No practical hazards beyond normal classroom rules
Graphs and photos only: no ice, warm water or fizzy drinks at the conference
Questions and feedback are about the science, never the people or their English
watch_out: Skills check first, strictly 15 minutes; survey fixed. Do not go through the answers in this lesson.
Talks run late on slow changeovers: present from own tables; next group stands at the bell.
'Not enough evidence yet' is an honest, respected verdict: say so in the opening.
Y9_W10.language_note: Students may read from the talk frame. Judge the science, not the English. 'Confidence' means evidence strength, not feeling.
Y9_W10.next_week: End of series: follow the close-out checklist (marking, tracker, awards, reports, gallery walk, kit back)
